title: Gilgamesh: the first hero in history
subtitle: Mesopotamia
subject: mythologie
description: King of Uruk, friend of Enkidu, hunter of immortality: the Epic of Gilgamesh, written 4,000 years ago, is humanity's oldest great story.

hero.hook: Before Homer, before the Bible: a king terrified of death travels to the end of the world, and brings back a lesson instead of eternity.

blocks.text: **Gilgamesh**, king of the city of **Uruk** in Mesopotamia, is the hero of the **Epic of Gilgamesh**. Carved on clay tablets more than **4,000 years** ago, the work comes before Homer and before the biblical stories.
It is not just an adventure. It is the story of a tyrant who discovers friendship, then the fear of dying, then a hard kind of wisdom: immortality is not in the body, but in what you leave behind.

sections.title: An epic pulled out of the sand

blocks.text: The text gathers older Sumerian tales. Its classic version, in Akkadian, is credited to the scribe [[Sîn-lēqi-unninni]], around the 12th century BC. Forgotten under the sand, it surfaced again in the 19th century in the library of King [[Ashurbanipal]] at **Nineveh**.

blocks.caption: Cuneiform tablet of the epic, British Museum

blocks.text: In **1872**, the Assyriologist **George Smith** deciphered at the British Museum a story of a flood, an ark and survival, roughly a thousand years older than Genesis. **Cuneiform** writing, pressed into clay, saved the text where papyrus would have vanished.
Reading the Flood tablet, George Smith is said to have been so excited that he began taking his clothes off in front of his stunned colleagues at the British Museum.

At the start, **Gilgamesh** is an unbearable king: two thirds god, one third human, and a tyrant to Uruk. To keep him in check, the goddess [[Aruru]] shapes **Enkidu**, a wild man who lives among the gazelles.

blocks.caption: Gilgamesh and Enkidu: from brawl to brotherly friendship

blocks.text: They fight, nobody wins, and the rivalry turns into friendship. Together they kill the monster **Humbaba** in the Cedar Forest, then the **Bull of Heaven** sent by the goddess **Ishtar**. The gods, angered, condemn Enkidu to die of illness. The death of his friend changes everything.

Standing over Enkidu's body, Gilgamesh understands that he too will die. He leaves his crown, wraps himself in animal skins and sets out to find **Utnapishtim**, the only man made immortal after the deluge described in the [[Flood narrative in the Epic]]. The journey takes him past the mountains of [[Mashu]] and across the Waters of Death.

blocks.caption: The Flood story: a thousand years before Noah, already written on clay

blocks.text: Utnapishtim sets him a test: stay awake for six days and seven nights. Gilgamesh falls asleep at once. Whoever cannot beat sleep will not beat death. He is shown a plant of youth, and a snake steals it while he bathes. The snake sheds its skin. The king goes home empty-handed.
This [[Flood narrative in the Epic]] comes about **1,000 years** before the biblical story of Noah: the same Mesopotamian background, in an older version.

sections.title: The eternity of the walls of Uruk

blocks.text: Back in **Uruk**, Gilgamesh looks at the ramparts of his city. The lesson is clear: biological immortality belongs to the gods. A human being lasts through his works and through the memory of the living.

Four thousand years later, the story still feeds world culture, from the biblical Noah to the monomyth theories of [[Joseph Campbell]]. To read Gilgamesh is to hear the first great human questions about death.
The **Epic of Gilgamesh**, **4,000 years** old, already contains a flood before the Bible. Its hero learns that immortality is not biological: it lies in the walls you build and the memory you leave.
